summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Côte d'Ivoire. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices records that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground.

Violence against LGBTQ people by non-state actors is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report counts three deaths within the community during that year. Police handling of such violence was described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often inclined to blame the victim, although authorities were dealing with complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Trans and gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man.

Peer-reviewed research published in 2015 found that travestis, people born male who live as women, endure harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender presentation does not attract attention. The same study reports that Ivoirian rights groups distanced themselves from travestis and left them underserved, and examines the isolation they experienced after the post-election violence of 2010–11.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, alteration of sex markers on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a trans identity, access to gender-affirming care, facility or bathroom rules, or the recognition of partners. The absence of those rules from the record is a gap in sourcing rather than a finding that they are unrestricted.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2011 human rights report on Côte d'Ivoire carries limited LGBT-specific content; its substance concerns the post-electoral crisis, which it records as leaving 3,000 people dead amid sexual violence and mass displacement. That crisis forms the backdrop against which the 2015 research situates travestis' isolation, and it indicates a period in which communal violence of any kind was met with weak state protection.

The 2015 study's central comparison is that gender normativity functions as a shield: sexual minorities who avoid visibility through their presentation experience less stigma than those who do not. A trans visitor, read as gender-nonconforming in public, falls on the unprotected side of that divide regardless of the legal position on same-sex conduct.

A New York Times article dated October 2024 addresses the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire, indicating continuing international attention on the country; the article's specific findings are not reproduced in the inventory.
localsOnly:
For resident LGBTQ and trans people, the recorded trend in police handling of complaints is a gradual improvement rather than a settled practice: authorities were described in 2023 as dealing with complaints somewhat better than in previous years, while responses to violence remained sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim.

Community organisations have not served all residents equally. The 2015 research found that Ivoirian rights groups distanced themselves from travestis, leaving the most visible and most targeted segment of the community without support even as they organised on behalf of others.

Three community deaths were recorded in 2023, a figure that sets the baseline of lethal risk faced by residents who remain in place rather than travelling through.
outOfScopeNotes:
The placement of transgender detainees — whether they are held in units matching birth sex or gender identity, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used — is not covered by any available publication. Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on this question for Côte d'Ivoire; on its country page, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

A UNDP report published in December 2024, reviewing ten years of African Commission Resolution 275, includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people. The specific findings of that overview are not stated in the available inventory and remain unresolved here.

Whether Côte d'Ivoire provides for legal gender recognition or amendment of sex markers on civil documents, and whether a visitor's entry documents are screened for such markers, is not sourced. Provisions on hate-crime aggravation, on partnership or marriage recognition, and on access to gender-affirming care are likewise not sourced from the inventory and should not be read as absent from the law.
